question: How do production agent systems stop an agent asserting false success, so The Architect stops making statements to the founder that are false?
decision_fed: The Architect truth gate: validate structured claims against the existing verification_evidence.db ledger instead of grading outbound prose; merge-track upstream hermes-agent issue #54722 / PR #54738 which is this exact gate, rather than writing a second one (LAW 3).
findings: False success is a measured failure class: 44-52% of all failures on tau2-bench, 75.8% on AppWorld, per-model 13-89% (arXiv 2606.09863). Receipt-checking against a runtime-written ledger detects 91% at 4% false positives versus 35% for regex word-lists (arXiv 2603.10060) — the word-list approach this estate already banned as proxy-grading is also the measurably losing one. Deterministic checks first (claim carries an evidence event id that must exist in SQLite with exit 0 and a timestamp after the last mutation), factored verifier model only for what the ledger cannot type. Upstream hermes-agent has the gate in flight: issue #54722, PR #54738.
metric: Share of outbound Architect status claims carrying a valid evidence event id; false-success rate on a replayed claim set.
metric_before: 0% of claims evidence-linked; live verification_evidence.db has 0 events; verify_on_stop OFF on the founder's only surface (Telegram).

question: What experience-accumulation patterns measurably make an agent improve, so maestro and The Architect learn fast with proof?
decision_fed: Maestro consult-before-escalate: fingerprint each problem, replay the last successful fix for a matching fingerprint before escalating, and a weekly learning receipt to Telegram proving what last week's escalations cost this week. Distill failures as well as successes (ReasoningBank result); promote a fix to a skill only after 2+ successful reuses.
findings: Distilled strategy memory from successes AND failures beats raw episodic memory: up to +34.2% effectiveness, -16% steps (ReasoningBank, arXiv 2509.25140). Skill libraries reach milestones 8.5-15.3x faster (Voyager). Proof of learning that survives workload drift: a frozen replay set of ~20 real past incidents re-run weekly — solved-count trend is the one metric immune to the workload changing under you. The everyday metrics: repeat-incident escalation rate declining, repeat resolution time versus first occurrence, memory hit rate.
metric: Weekly learning receipt: fraction of last week's escalation fingerprints auto-resolved this week; repeat-incident median resolution time versus first occurrence; frozen replay set solved-count.
metric_before: maestro consults nothing before escalating; one Stripe finding escalated 46 times in 29h with zero learning between passes; skills/shapes tables held 0 rows until PR #4.

question: What should the estate's asset catalogue, agent registry and observability actually be built on, given no funds, LAW 19 portability and LAW 34 provider agnosticism?
decision_fed: Catalogue and inventory go in SQLite, served read-only by Datasette and replicated by Litestream to object storage, roughly $3-6/month on Fly. Instrumentation is OpenTelemetry OTLP with the GenAI semantic conventions, collected by self-hosted Langfuse (MIT core). Agent identity and discovery use A2A Agent Cards at /.well-known/agent-card.json plus MCP for tool access. Infrastructure as code is OpenTofu, not Terraform. Artifacts are OCI with CycloneDX SBOMs. REFUSED: every seat-priced internal developer portal (Port, Cortex, OpsLevel, Roadie, Compass) because a one-founder estate pays per seat for a directory it can write itself; Humanitec, whose CLI and Terraform provider ship no licence file at all, which under LAW 40 test 3 grants nothing; LangSmith and Braintrust, whose exit is a support ticket; anything requiring Kubernetes; and Backstage as a runtime, because its plugin system is mid-migration and the maintenance cost lands on one person.
findings: Backstage is the reference catalogue but its frontend system migration means a self-hosted instance is a standing maintenance job, so take its catalogue MODEL and not its runtime. Every hosted portal in the survey prices per developer or per service, which is the wrong shape for one founder and six sessions. Humanitec ships no LICENSE file in either its CLI or its Terraform provider, so nothing it produces can be resold. OpenTelemetry now has GenAI semantic conventions and an entities data model, which makes agent traces portable across vendors and is the single largest lock-in escape available. Langfuse's core is MIT and self-hostable; its licence key gates only enterprise features. A2A Agent Cards give agent discovery a published standard, so the agent registry does not need to be invented here. OpenTofu is the fork with a live release cadence after IBM's HashiCorp acquisition and HashiCorp's BUSL licence change.

question: What does the DORA 2025 research say about AI-assisted delivery that should change how this estate works?
decision_fed: Two changes. Treat the founder's complaint as the primary platform signal (user-centricity is the strongest reported driver of product quality), which became LAW 36. And stop treating trust in AI output as given: 39.2% of DORA respondents report little or no trust in AI, which is the same instinct behind the founder's 'I don't trust anything you say' and behind THE FOUR HARD RULES. Verification before assertion is not local pedantry, it is the measured industry condition.
findings: Organisations that prioritise end user experience produce higher quality products and have more productive developers. Trust in AI is the binding constraint on AI leverage, not capability: those who trust generative AI use it more, and 39.2% report little or no trust. Platform engineering shows up as an amplifier, meaning it multiplies whatever the underlying practice already is, good or bad.

question: Prospector stack: is the POPDD gate/receipt chain reinventing hook managers, in-toto attestation, or CI?
findings: POPDD receipts are HMAC-SHA256 with one symmetric key in an untracked .pem - internal consistency only, no third-party verifiability; in-toto/Sigstore/SLSA do this asymmetrically with a transparency log but assume CI OIDC, and none expresses a local staged-diff commit gate, so the gate is half-reinvention half-genuine-gap. GitHub meters self-hosted runners from 2026-03-01 at $0.002/min except public repos. pytest-testmon would under-select here: the suite has proven cross-file global-state coupling (_MOAT_PRIMARY, --dist loadfile).

question: What open-source tooling should carry the estate's data collection and plumbing, given one laptop, no budget, and a requirement that every dependency permit commercial resale?
decision_fed: DuckDB + DuckLake v1.0 with a SQLite catalog + plain Parquet + fastjsonschema contracts + ~30 lines of SQL assertions + dlt for the API-shaped sources; SQLite FTS5 kept for transcript search only. Two new dependencies, MIT and BSD-3, zero servers. Rejected dbt-core (alpha v2, solves a team problem we do not have), SQLMesh (protects downstream consumers we do not have), Great Expectations (18 deps for four SQL statements), Meltano (venv-per-tap to read local files), Iceberg (no server-free local write path), and DuckDB fts as the transcript index (its own docs say the index does not update on append). Filed as crew#74.
findings: Four candidate tools fail the resale test outright and were disqualified on licence, not on merit: Soda Core relicensed Apache-2.0 to Elastic License 2.0 on 2026-01-27 and its PyPI classifier now reads Proprietary; Airbyte is ELv2 and its abctl installer now brings Docker, kind, Kubernetes, Helm and nginx; Sling is GPL-3.0 with the useful features behind Sling Pro; ingestr is FSL-1.1. ParadeDB pg_search is AGPL-3.0 by deliberate choice and Typesense is a GPL-3.0 server. The dbt Fusion binary is proprietary under dbt Labs' Product Licensing Agreement even though dbt-core is Apache-2.0, and the archived dbt-labs/dbt-fusion repo is still mostly ELv2. Governance: Fivetran completed its dbt Labs merger 2026-06-01, became steward of Great Expectations 2026-05-13, and donated SQLMesh to the Linux Foundation around 2026-03, so dbt, GX and SQLMesh are now all downstream of one commercial parent. DuckLake reached v1.0 in April 2026, MIT, production-ready with backward-compatibility guarantees, catalog in a SQLite file and data in plain Parquet, which satisfies LAW 19 by construction rather than by remembering to run an export drill. The 76k transcripts need byte-offset resumption, which no tool in the field provides: dlt's filesystem source keys on modification time, so a transcript appended to while a session is live is re-read whole and duplicated, and it lists the entire tree before applying the glob.

question: Does the Collate Community License actually bar this estate from using OpenMetadata, and did the same reasoning error affect Soda Core, Airbyte, ingestr and Sling?
why: The founder read the clause I had cited and asked 'are we competing? i dont think so'. He was right, and the answer invalidates a decision already recorded in this ledger.
findings: Collate CCL v1.0 section 1.1 grants use, modification, distribution and copying. The only carve-out is the Excluded Purpose: making available a SaaS, PaaS, IaaS or similar online service that competes with Collate products or services that provide the Software. Running the catalog over our own estate is none of those, so the clause is not engaged.

Elastic License 2.0 has the same shape: it bars providing the software to third parties as a managed service, and bars circumventing licence key functionality. Internal use is unrestricted. Soda Core and Airbyte are therefore usable.
FSL-1.1 bars competing use for two years and then converts to Apache 2.0. Internal use is permitted throughout. ingestr is usable.

GPL-3.0 is the only licence in the set with teeth against this estate, and they are in distribution rather than use: a derivative work shipped inside a sold platform must be released under GPL. Sling is the one to think about, and I had ranked it as the least severe.
CCL section 1.4 forbids sublicensing, so a buyer of this platform would take the CCL directly from Collate rather than through us. That is a diligence footnote under LAW 40, not a bar.
decision_fed: Corrects the earlier row in this ledger that recorded OpenMetadata and Soda Core as refused on licence grounds. The correct verdict is: permitted for internal use, permitted inside a sold platform with notice and no sublicensing, barred only as a hosted service competing with the vendor. OpenMetadata remains refused on weight alone, measured at 194 inventory rows with 10 descriptions -- a field nobody fills is not fixed by a catalog. The stack choice of DuckDB plus DuckLake plus fastjsonschema is unaffected because it was never made on licence grounds.
class_of_error: I graded each licence against 'could we sell this tool' when LAW 40 asks 'could we sell the platform we build with it'. Those questions have different answers. The pipeline build now carries a three-question grade per dependency: can we run it, can a buyer take it, could we ever host it against its vendor.

question: Which parts of this estate are bespoke code doing a job a recognised tool already does, and what is the maturity evidence a buyer would accept for each replacement?
why: Founder, 2026-08-24: 'we thik we can cod our way our of anything', 'w reinvesting the wheel and doing a terirbe job', 'an investor would lik to know our franework and toolig is nature'. Maturity is the deliverable, not just working code.
findings: CNCF maturity, read out of landscape.yml directly rather than from a vendor page: Open Policy Agent carries 'project: graduated', Backstage carries 'project: incubating'. Trivy, Syft, Grype and Kratix appear in the landscape with no 'project:' field at all, which means landscape-listed and NOT a CNCF project. Calling any of those four 'CNCF' on a diligence page would be a false claim.
Licences, exact SPDX from the GitHub API: Backstage Apache-2.0, Datasette Apache-2.0, OPA Apache-2.0, Kratix Apache-2.0, Trivy Apache-2.0, Syft Apache-2.0, Grype Apache-2.0, ORT Apache-2.0.

conftest reports SPDX NOASSERTION. Its LICENSE text is Apache-2.0 but carries a custom preamble that defeats GitHub's detector. A buyer's licence scanner will flag it, so the answer belongs in the docs before they ask.

humanitec/terraform-provider-humanitec has license: null and no LICENSE or COPYING file in the repo root. Verified from two angles, the licence API and the contents listing. No licence file grants nothing, so that dependency is unusable in anything sold.

SARIF upload to GitHub code scanning needs a paid Code Security licence on private repositories. The zero-cost path for supply-chain findings is dependency-snapshot plus an artifact upload plus a non-zero exit code, never SARIF.

ORT is the only genuinely foundation-governed licence-compliance tool in the set (Linux Foundation / ACT), but it needs a JVM and ships no Homebrew formula, so adopting it costs setup that Syft and Grype do not.

The bespoke risk-register check was 80 lines of Python implementing rules a policy engine already does: required fields, allowed values, a claim that needs a receipt. Seven of its rules moved to Rego unchanged.

Rego cannot read the filesystem, by design, which is what makes untrusted policy safe to run. So 'does the program this receipt names exist on PATH' cannot move to policy. The split is real rather than tidy: seven structural rules moved, one filesystem rule stayed in Python.
decision_fed: Adopted conftest and OPA for the risk register's rules: policy/risk_register.rego plus scripts/verify.d/86-risk-policy.sh, merged in PR #77. The Python check scripts/verify.d/85-risk-register.sh is retained as the fallback rather than deleted, per the founder's instruction to keep what gets replaced. Both were run over the same three broken registers and agreed on every one. Cost is zero: brew install, Apache-2.0, no account, no network call.
metric: rules in the risk register check that a recognised engine enforces rather than our own Python
metric_after: 7 of 8, with the 8th impossible in Rego and kept in the retained fallback

question: Is the developer portal this estate just deployed something an investor would call industry standard, and what are the free options if Backstage stops being viable?
why: Founder, 2026-08-24: 'an investor would lik to know our franework and toolig is nature', and separately 'we nust always have options switachble in 10 seconds', 'if we lost backdoo, we nust have a fallback'.
findings: Backstage is CNCF Incubating, not Graduated. Accepted to Sandbox 2020-09-08, advanced to Incubating 2022-03-15, which is still its most recent stage change. Four angles agreed: landscape.yml, cncf.io/projects, the CLOMonitor API and Backstage's own docs. Saying 'Graduated' on a diligence page would be a false claim.

Backstage is Apache-2.0, 34,218 stars, latest release v1.54.3 on 2026-08-22, 290 named adopters in ADOPTERS.md including American Airlines, Expedia, LinkedIn, Twilio, Siemens, Volvo Cars, Booking.com, Fidelity and Mercedes-Benz.io.
Governance is vendor-concentrated under neutral ownership: Spotify holds 4 of the 5 core maintainer seats and the top three committers are all Spotify. State it rather than let a buyer find it.

The maintenance-burden criticism is real and has named authors. Spotify's own head of engineering for Backstage told The New Stack in 2023 that average adoption sits at 10 percent. A Distinguished Engineer at SPS Commerce told InfoQ in 2025 that Backstage is a framework for building a portal, not a portal. Roadie's 2025 survey of 105 practitioners puts self-hosted setups at 3 to 12 full-time engineers, though Roadie sells managed Backstage so it is a vendor source.

The widely repeated Gartner figures of '2-5 FTEs' and '$150K per 20 developers' trace to a vendor CEO's blog citing Gartner secondhand. The Gartner note itself is paywalled and unread. Do not repeat those as Gartner findings.
Thoughtworks Technology Radar has Backstage at Adopt since Vol 27 in October 2022 and has never placed it in Hold. There is no Thoughtworks caution to cite either way.

Datasette is Apache-2.0 and current at 0.65.3, but it is a single-maintainer project with no foundation: 2,910 commits from Simon Willison against 20 from the next human contributor. Sound as a fallback renderer, not presentable as an industry-standard portal.

Only four options in the whole survey are self-hostable at genuinely zero cost: Backstage, Datasette, Kratix and OpenChoreo, all Apache-2.0. Port, Cortex, Roadie and Humanitec have no free self-hosted tier at all. Port's free tier is hosted SaaS capped at 15 seats; Cortex publishes no price; Humanitec starts at 1,999 euros a month.

OpenChoreo is the strongest free fallback and is Backstage-adjacent rather than a rival: CNCF Sandbox since 2026-01-06, Apache-2.0, WSO2-built, and it ships a Backstage-powered portal. It scores better than Backstage on both public health scanners, CLOMonitor 86.0 against 74.4 and OpenSSF Scorecard 7.5 against 6.3. The caveat is age: the repo was created 2025-02-28 and its top three contributors are all WSO2.
The deployed Backstage is 1.54.0, released 2026-08-18. Current is 1.54.3, released 2026-08-22. Three patch releases behind.
decision_fed: Keep Backstage as the portal and Datasette as the independent fallback renderer, and describe Backstage to a buyer as CNCF Incubating rather than Graduated. Record OpenChoreo as the named replacement if Backstage stops being viable, since it is free, Apache-2.0 and carries the same portal. Record two risk-register rows a buyer would otherwise find themselves: Datasette's single maintainer, and Spotify's concentration of Backstage maintainer seats.
metric: portal components whose maturity claim is backed by a source a stranger can re-read
metric_after: 2 of 2, Backstage at CNCF Incubating and Datasette at single-maintainer with the commit counts

question: If the estate leaves Fly.io for Kubernetes, which distribution, GitOps controller, policy engine and self-healing components should carry it, and which of them can survive a buyer checking their maturity and licence?
why: Founder, 2026-08-24: 'look you eed to swrich tacts, and reseach k's', 'ad tooling for autination, total self healing prod ready', and 12 minutes later 'we dont eforce stadard adbest practices, this is a new funxtion, we need to be ready fron day 0 thats why ii asked for research, stop naking ecuses'. Second time he has asked for research on this, which is itself the defect signal LAW 16 names.
findings: Three components a naive Kubernetes design would call industry standard are not CNCF Graduated, and a buyer checks. k3s is CNCF SANDBOX, not graduated, in landscape.yml. Velero is SANDBOX on both landscape.yml and CLOMonitor (83.6). External Secrets Operator is SANDBOX on CLOMonitor (96.9). Talos Linux is NOT A CNCF PROJECT AT ALL. Saying any of the four is graduated on a diligence page would be a false claim, exactly as 'Backstage is Graduated' would have been.

What IS graduated, confirmed by two angles (landscape.yml and the CLOMonitor API): Kubernetes, Argo, Flux, Kyverno, cert-manager, Crossplane, OPA and Prometheus. CLOMonitor scores: cert-manager 95.65, Kyverno 93.75, Argo 93.21, Crossplane 88.54.

Kyverno graduated 2026-03-24, which makes policy-as-code a graduated-tier answer to the founder's complaint that the estate does not enforce standards. Policies are ordinary Kubernetes YAML with CEL as the expression language since v1.17, so there is no Rego to learn, and it validates, mutates, generates and verifies images. OPA Gatekeeper is the alternative and wins only on cross-platform reuse, because Rego also runs against Terraform and plain APIs. Both Apache-2.0.

Licences are clean everywhere except one, checked against the GitHub API rather than a README. Apache-2.0: k3s, Argo CD, Flux, Kyverno, Gatekeeper, cert-manager, Velero, External Secrets, Cluster API, Crossplane, Litestream, Kured, kind. Talos Linux is MPL-2.0, which is weak copyleft at file level and does not reach a product built on it. Sidero's Omni reports NOASSERTION on the GitHub API, which is BUSL: self-hosting is non-production only until it converts to MPL four years after release.

Argo CD and Flux are both CNCF Graduated and both Apache-2.0, so the choice is not a maturity question. Argo CD is 23,978 stars against Flux's 8,367, runs in about 60 percent of Kubernetes clusters per the 2025 Argo CD end user survey, and ships a web UI and centralised RBAC. Flux is a modular set of controllers with no UI, which makes it easier to bootstrap programmatically and leaves nothing extra to secure or expose.

'Self-healing' in Kubernetes is four separate layers and only the first is free. Layer 1, the built-in one: liveness and readiness probes, restart policy and rescheduling off a failed node. Layer 2, drift correction: Argo CD selfHeal true, which reverts anything that diverges from git. Layer 3, node repair: node-problem-detector for hardware, kernel and OOM conditions, Kured for safe reboots after patching. Layer 4, bad deploys: Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery with automatic rollback. Named limit from the sources: built-in primitives only fix failures whose remedy is restart, replace or rescale. They cannot fix a bad deploy, a leaked credential, a poisoned cache or a downstream outage, and only layers 2 and 4 touch those.

Cluster API and Crossplane are not competitors and picking one of them as 'the provider-agnostic layer' is the common error. Cluster API is a Kubernetes SIG subproject scoped to cluster lifecycle across infrastructure providers. Crossplane is a broader control plane for any cloud resource. Both graduated-tier, both Apache-2.0, and the sources describe them as used together rather than instead of each other.

SQLite is the binding constraint on any Kubernetes design for this shop and it is not solved by Kubernetes. SQLite does 10,000 to 50,000 writes per second and 100,000 plus reads per second on NVMe but permits exactly one writer, so the API tier cannot be replicated. The pattern is a single-replica StatefulSet with Recreate strategy and a Litestream sidecar for continuous replication. Litestream is Apache-2.0 and publishes a Kubernetes guide. Until the store moves off SQLite, 'highly available' is a word this estate may not use about the shop.

Cost at rest, two sources: Hetzner with Talos, Cilium and WireGuard at about 14 euros a month, and a second source at about 10 euros. Neither is measured by this estate and both are one angle. The current Fly bill is the number that matters and it is not in this row.
decision_fed: k3s on a rented Linux box, not Talos, and the reason is the operator rather than the technology: Talos has no SSH and no shell by design, which removes the entire debugging surface on the night something breaks with one operator and zero prior Kubernetes experience. Talos is recorded as the named upgrade path once the estate has run k3s for a quarter. Argo CD over Flux, because selfHeal true is the literal thing the founder asked for in one line, and because Argo ships a UI a buyer can open, which LAW 41 requires and Flux structurally cannot give. Flux is the named replacement if Argo stops being viable. Kyverno for standards enforcement from day 0, graduated and CLOMonitor 93.75, answering the complaint directly. cert-manager for TLS. Velero and External Secrets adopted but declared SANDBOX wherever their maturity is stated. Single-replica StatefulSet plus Litestream for the SQLite store, and no HA claim about the API tier while SQLite is the store.
metric: shop components whose maturity claim is backed by a source a stranger can re-read, and whose recovery from deletion is timed rather than asserted
metric_before: 0 of 6 components have a maturity source; 0 self-healing claims have a measured recovery time
metric_after: 6 of 6 components carry a landscape.yml or CLOMonitor maturity and a GitHub API licence; recovery time pending the drill in deploy/rehearse_cluster.sh

question: Which open-source data-quality tool can gate this estate's SQLite warehouse in under 60 seconds, with a licence that survives a sale of the platform?
decision_fed: https://github.com/chidionyema/crew/issues/84 -- keep the hand-written sqlite3 runner over the ODCS contracts, and do not adopt a second contract format on day 0
findings: Great Expectations 1.x has no data-validation command line at all; its __main__.py states it never touches data, so it cannot produce an exit code without a wrapper we would have to maintain.

There is no working dbt to SQLite path today: dbt-sqlite 1.10.0 pins dbt-adapters ~=1.16 while dbt-core 1.12.3 requires >=1.24.5, which is unsatisfiable, and pip silently back-solves to a 1.4.0 that dies on import.

question: Before hand-writing three more law-to-check rows in science/enforcement-map.json, does an off-the-shelf requirements-traceability tool already do law-to-guard mapping better?
decision_fed: https://github.com/chidionyema/crew/issues/105 -- keep the existing hand-rolled enforcement-map.json + map_covers_laws.py schema for the LAW 33/43/44 rows rather than adopting a traceability tool
findings: shtracer (MIT, 301 commits) tags requirements inline in source files with a comment syntax and compiles a JSON traceability graph, but it has no concept of a check's live/dead state on disk -- it would still need this repo's own law_enforcement.py to answer whether a bound check actually runs.

ReqView stores requirements as git-tracked JSON, which is the property this repo already has for free in enforcement-map.json, but its licence is per-seat commercial and it has no notion of a mechanical/partial/judgement verdict, which is the axis map_covers_laws.py actually gates on.

TestCollab's RTM maps requirements to test cases, not to arbitrary shell/CI guards, so LAW 33/43/44's checks -- a GitHub Actions job and a Python regex gate -- would still need a custom adapter written by hand either way.
None of the three researched tools reduces the change to less than the 36-line JSON diff this PR ships, and two of the three add a licence or a per-seat cost the estate does not have today.
metric: lines of new tooling introduced to close crew#105's fourth checklist box
metric_after: 36 (three JSON entries in the existing schema, zero new dependencies)
